source: Somsak Wannasaree, "Banana Orchards" (Khmer translation, 1997), section 11 (ripening banana)
text:
Banana is a self-ripening (climacteric) fruit — once cut, it continues to ripen on its own because it produces its own ripening gas (ethylene). This source describes several ways growers and traders control and speed up that process:

Ethylene gas method: fruit is held in a space with temperature controlled at roughly 20-21°C (not exceeding about 24°C), then exposed to ethylene gas diluted to about a 1:1000 ratio with air for 12-24 hours. Humidity is then kept around 80% for a further 3-4 days to complete ripening.

Smoke method: banana is placed in an enclosed container along with smoke from burning banana leaves or plant trash; the smoke contains natural ethylene-like compounds that trigger ripening. The container is sealed to trap the smoke, and under good temperature control (cited around 17°C for this variant) this can ripen close to 90% of a batch evenly.

Carbide (calcium carbide) method: carbide reacts with moisture in the air to release acetylene gas, which mimics the natural ripening trigger. Fruit is sealed in a container with a small amount of carbide, held at roughly 12-14°C, and typically ripens within about 3-4 days.

Natural (room) method: fruit is simply left in a well-ventilated but enclosed space — for example wrapped in paper or cloth, or lightly covered in rice husk or straw to help trap the fruit's own natural ethylene — without any added gas or chemical. This takes longer, roughly 7-10 days depending on climate and season, but is considered to preserve the most natural flavor since nothing artificial is added.

For any of these methods, consistent temperature control matters more than the specific ripening agent used — uneven temperature during the ripening period is the most common cause of blotchy or uneven ripening in a batch.
